payload.prompt: What does the spotter mean?

audio.description: A spotter's voice saying "Clear high" over team radio.

options.text: No one above; you can move up safely.
The upper lane is blocked.
Go faster in the high groove.

explanation.correct: Right. "Clear high" means the high lane is open and the driver can move up safely.
explanation.incorrect: Spotters use short calls: "Clear high" means the upper lane is open and available.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: The spotter said he was clear and he moved up and got hit.

options.text: Either the spotter missed someone or communication failed; spotters are human.
Spotters never make mistakes.
Drivers ignore spotters.

payload.translation: Spotters do their best but are human and can miss a car.

followUps.line: Spotters watch blind spots but radio failures or missed cars happen rarely.
followUps.why: It's a split-second job at 180 mph.

followUps.line: The driver has to hear and act immediately too.
followUps.why: Two people have to execute perfectly for a call to work.

payload.prompt: What is the spotter's primary job?

options.text: To watch the pit crew and verify tires.
To watch from above and call out nearby cars and safe lanes.
To track fuel and tell the driver when to pit.

explanation.correct: Right. The spotter sits on the roof with a radio and calls out every car nearby. It's a second set of eyes.
explanation.incorrect: The spotter is a team member on the roof. They call out cars and danger. Without them, drivers cannot see the sides, back or above.

payload.prompt: Is a spotter necessary for driver safety?

scene.alt: A driver in the cockpit cannot see behind or sides.

explanation.correct: Spotters are critical. Drivers have huge blind spots. Spotters are essential.
explanation.incorrect: Spotters are vital. Without them, blind-spot crashes and wrecks spike. They are not optional.

payload.prompt: "Car {{side}}," means {{meaning}}.

explanation.correct: Perfect. "Car left" warns about a car on the left side.
explanation.incorrect: Spotters use short calls. "Car left" warns about a nearby car on the left.

lessons.title: Reading the loop data
lessons.objective: Read laps led and average running position.

payload.prompt: What does loop data tell you?

options.text: Only finishing position.
Average running position and speed; who was truly fast.
How many pit stops a driver made.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Loop data shows the car's pace through the race, not just where it finished.
explanation.incorrect: Loop data strips away luck to show you true speed and performance over the entire race.

payload.prompt: Led 180 of 400 laps. How many laps did others lead?

explanation.correct: Right. 400 minus 180 equals 220. Dominance on track does not always mean a win.
explanation.incorrect: If one driver led 180 of 400 laps, others led 220 total. Leading most laps does not guarantee victory.

payload.prompt: {{stat}} shows {{meaning}}.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Laps led shows dominance. Many laps led means a fast car.
explanation.incorrect: Laps led is a sign of a dominant car. It shows speed through the race.

payload.prompt: Led 250 laps and had the best loop data but finished second. What happened?

options.text: The driver made a mistake near the end.
The car was fastest but a caution or pit call cost them victory.
The driver was not that good.

explanation.correct: Laps led and loop data say the car was dominant. Late-race events (caution or pit strategy) changed the outcome.
explanation.incorrect: When you see most laps led but a second-place finish, a caution or strategy call cost them. The car was fastest.

payload.prompt: Driver A led 200 laps with the best average position. Driver B finished first, led 20 laps. Who had the faster car?

options.label: Driver A had the faster car.
options.consequence: Data shows Driver A dominated. Driver B won by strategy. Both are true.

options.label: Driver B had the faster car.
options.consequence: Driver B won but the stats show Driver A was faster most of the race.

payload.expertNote: Speed dominance and race victory are not the same. Fans who read loop data see the full picture.

lessons.title: Dominant but did not win
lessons.objective: Explain why the fastest car does not always win.

payload.prompt: Fastest car, led 200 laps, finished fifth after a late caution. Is this "taken away"?

options.label: Unlucky; the fastest car didn't win.
options.consequence: The data supports it. He was dominant. A caution cost him. That's racing.

options.label: They blew the pit strategy.
options.consequence: Also true. A better call might have helped. But both can be true.

payload.expertNote: The fastest car does not always win. Strategy and luck matter. Smart fans understand this.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: He led the whole race and got second. How?

options.text: A caution or pit strategy cost him despite having the fastest car.
He made a huge mistake.
His car was not really that good.

payload.translation: Leading and having the fastest car is not the same as winning.

followUps.line: A caution or pit call can shuffle everything. Speed is one force; strategy and luck are others.
Fans who understand this do not blame the driver for losing with the best car.

payload.prompt: Does the fastest car always win?

scene.alt: A lap chart showing a fast car that led early but faded late.

explanation.correct: Right. Speed is one force among many. Cautions, pit strategy and track position matter hugely.
explanation.incorrect: The fastest car does not always win. Cautions, pit calls and track position shift races. Speed is necessary but not sufficient.

payload.prompt: What often matters more than raw speed late in a race?

options.text: The driver's experience level.
Track position. Being in front beats speed late.
The pit crew size.

explanation.correct: Track position is huge. A car in front with a 2-second lead can hold off a faster car. Passing is hard.
explanation.incorrect: Track position—being in front—is a huge advantage. A faster car behind has to find a way around. That's why pit strategy focuses on track position.

payload.prompt: Winning takes {{factor1}}, {{factor2}} and {{factor3}}.

explanation.correct: Perfect. A three-legged stool: speed, strategy and luck. All three matter.
explanation.incorrect: Speed is necessary but not enough. Strategy and luck decide races. It takes all three.

payload.prompt: Does a damaged car have unlimited repair time?

scene.alt: A damaged car being worked on in garage.

explanation.correct: Right. The damaged vehicle policy has a clock. Teams get limited time or they are done.
explanation.incorrect: The damaged vehicle policy limits repair time. If the clock runs out, the team is finished for the day.

payload.prompt: Why does NASCAR have a damaged vehicle time limit?

options.text: To keep races on schedule and prevent garage hiding.
To punish teams for crashing.
To make wrecker trucks work more.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The policy keeps races efficient. Without it, teams could hide in the garage forever.
explanation.incorrect: The damaged vehicle policy keeps races flowing. It forces a decision: fix it fast or go home.

payload.prompt: If repair time runs out, the team {{result}}.
payload.template: If repair time runs out, the team {{result}}.

explanation.correct: Right. The clock is final. No time left means done for the day.
explanation.incorrect: The damaged vehicle policy is strict. If the clock runs out and the car is not ready, the team is finished.

payload.prompt: Wreck needs 12 min to fix. Clock allows 10 min. 100 laps left. What do you do?

options.label: Go home; can't beat the clock.
options.consequence: You accepted reality. The rule is the rule. A bad fix might not work.

options.label: Rush and try a partial fix.
options.consequence: High-risk. Might work. Might not. It's a gamble.

payload.expertNote: The damaged vehicle policy is strict. When the clock runs out, it's over.

payload.prompt: What are common NASCAR penalties?

options.text: Points loss, crew chief suspension, fines.
Only fines; no suspensions.
Automatic disqualification for any violation.

explanation.correct: NASCAR has an arsenal: points loss, crew chief suspensions, fines and position penalties. Penalties vary by violation.
explanation.incorrect: Penalties range from fines to crew chief suspension to points loss. Inspection failures can be devastating.

payload.prompt: Can a team lose a race win in inspection?

scene.alt: Tech inspectors checking a race car.

explanation.correct: Yes. Post-race inspection failure costs the win, points and more. Inspection is serious.
explanation.incorrect: A post-race inspection failure can overturn a win. It has happened. Inspection is final.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: His crew chief got suspended. That's brutal.

options.text: A crew chief suspension is huge because the crew chief calls strategy and adjustments.
Crew chiefs don't matter much to results.
Suspensions are never given.

payload.translation: Crew chief suspensions are tough because strategy is often as important as speed.

followUps.line: The crew chief makes pit calls and adjustments. Losing them for one race hurts.
Fans see it as karma if the team broke rules, but also as a big swing.
followUps.why: It has real impact on the championship.

payload.prompt: A {{penalty-type}} penalty hurts because {{reason}}.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Crew chief suspensions hurt because that person is irreplaceable in the moment.
explanation.incorrect: Crew chief suspensions hurt because a backup is never as sharp on real-time calls.

payload.prompt: What does NASCAR inspection focus on?

options.text: Only engine and fuel.
Everything: body, weight, aero, engine, fuel.
Safety gear only.

explanation.correct: Inspection is thorough. Every part is checked using precision tools. A millimeter off is a violation.
explanation.incorrect: NASCAR inspection is comprehensive. Dimensions, weight, aero parts, engine specs—all checked. Rules are tight.

lessons.title: Reading a race from the lap chart
lessons.objective: Read a race from its chart.

payload.prompt: Put these race events in order.

items.text: Lap 1: race begins in qualifying order.
Lap 60: stage break, first pit cycle.
Lap 62: order shuffles; pit winners lead.
Lap 120: stage break, second pit cycle.

explanation.correct: Perfect. A lap chart shows how the running order changes. Pit cycles reorder the field.
explanation.incorrect: A lap chart shows position changes lap by lap. Pit cycles are the key moments when the field reshuffles.

payload.prompt: What can a lap chart tell you that commentary misses?

options.text: Exact pit stop times and fuel savings.
Who was fast, who gained on pit road, when cautions happened.
Only final positions.

explanation.correct: A lap chart shows the complete race narrative. Who led when, who moved up, who faded. Commentary misses details.
explanation.incorrect: Reading a lap chart is like reading a race's DNA. You see every position change and pit cycle effect.

payload.prompt: On a lap chart, who won the pit cycle?

options.text: Car that leaves pit road first or ahead.
Car with the youngest crew chief.
Car that pitted earliest in the day.

explanation.correct: A pit-cycle winner exits pit road first or best. They gain track position on rivals.
explanation.incorrect: When multiple cars pit together, the one that exits first wins the cycle. The lap chart shows it clearly.

payload.prompt: A lap chart tracks {{what}} and shows {{reveals}}.
payload.template: A lap chart tracks {{what}} and shows {{reveals}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A lap chart is a position story. Pit cycles are when the field reshapes.
explanation.incorrect: Reading a lap chart means seeing where each car ran at each lap. Pit cycles reshape everything.

payload.prompt: Driver A led. After pit cycle, Driver B exits pit road first. What happened?

facts.label: Pit stop result
facts.value: Driver B exits pit road first

options.label: Driver B's pit crew won.
options.consequence: Driver B gained track position through a quicker stop. It's a pit win.

options.label: Driver A made a mistake.
options.consequence: Maybe, but the chart shows B exited first. Don't assume blame. Just read the position shift.

payload.expertNote: Pit cycles are where races are won. Lap charts show exactly who gained on pit road.
